defaults.reviewNotes: Claude-authored and self-checked against standard references; pending independent expert verification.

questions.scenario: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks and orbit about 20,000 km up, moving at nearly 4 km per second.
questions.question: Compared with identical clocks on the ground, do the satellite clocks tick faster or slower?
questions.reveal: Faster, by about 38 microseconds a day.
questions.explanation: Two relativity effects compete. The satellites' speed makes their clocks run slow by about 7 microseconds a day (special relativity). But they sit in weaker gravity, which makes them run fast by about 45 microseconds a day (general relativity). Gravity wins: net, about 38 microseconds a day fast. Light travels over 11 km in that time, so engineers set the satellite clocks' frequency slightly low before launch to compensate.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Moving clocks run slow' is the famous rule, so the fast satellites seem certain to lag.
questions.principle: Clocks run faster in weaker gravity and slower when moving fast; for GPS the gravitational effect is larger.
questions.funFact: The satellite clocks are tuned to about 10.22999999543 MHz on the ground so they tick at 10.23 MHz in orbit.
questions.source: Ashby (2003), 'Relativity in the Global Positioning System', Living Reviews in Relativity

questions.scenario: Many Wi-Fi networks use radio waves around 2.4 GHz, very close to the 2.45 GHz used by microwave ovens.
questions.question: Why doesn't Wi-Fi warm you up the way a microwave oven heats food?
options: It's a different kind of radiation
Its power is far lower and spread out
questions.reveal: Its power is far lower and spreads out in all directions.
questions.explanation: It's the same kind of radio wave; the difference is power. A microwave oven pumps around 1,000 watts into a small metal box that traps it. A Wi-Fi router transmits a fraction of a watt, spread out in all directions, and the intensity falls off rapidly with distance. The power reaching your body is millions of times weaker than inside an oven, so any heating is negligible.
questions.intuitionTrap: Same frequency seems like it should mean the same effect.
questions.principle: Heating depends on absorbed power, and radiated intensity falls with the square of distance.
questions.funFact: A running microwave oven can disrupt nearby 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, because a little of its energy leaks out on the same band.

questions.scenario: You delete a file from a traditional spinning hard drive and empty the recycle bin.
questions.question: Is the file's data immediately wiped from the disk?
options: Usually not; the space is marked free
It moves to a hidden folder
questions.reveal: Usually not: the space is just marked as free.
questions.explanation: Deleting usually removes the file's entry from the drive's index and marks its space as available. The actual bits stay put until something new is written over them, which is why recovery tools can often bring files back. SSDs complicate things: with the TRIM command, the drive is told which blocks are free and may erase them in the background, so deleted files on SSDs are often unrecoverable soon afterwards.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Delete' sounds like the data is destroyed.
questions.principle: File systems track where data lives; deleting usually removes the pointer, not the data.
questions.funFact: That's why secure-erase tools overwrite data, and why discarded drives are often physically shredded.

questions.scenario: Your laptop has 16 GB of RAM and a 512 GB SSD. You shut it down completely and unplug it.
questions.question: What happens to the data that was in RAM?
questions.explanation: Ordinary RAM stores each bit as a tiny electric charge that leaks away within milliseconds, so it must be constantly refreshed. Cut the power and the refreshing stops, and the contents fade away. That's why unsaved work disappears in a power cut. An SSD stores data in cells that trap charge for years without power, so your files survive.
questions.intuitionTrap: Memory sounds like something that should remember.
questions.principle: DRAM is volatile memory and needs power and refreshing; flash storage is non-volatile.
questions.caveat: Hibernate mode does copy RAM to storage before powering off, and very cold RAM can hold traces for seconds to minutes.
questions.funFact: Security researchers have frozen RAM chips with canned air to recover encryption keys from them, a 'cold boot attack'.

questions.scenario: Processor A runs at 4 GHz. Processor B runs at 3 GHz.
questions.question: Is processor A necessarily faster?
options: Yes, more GHz is always faster
questions.explanation: Clock speed is how many cycles a processor runs per second, not how much work it does per cycle. Different designs complete different amounts of work each cycle, have different numbers of cores, different caches and different memory speeds. A chip running at 3 GHz that does twice as much per cycle beats a 4 GHz chip that does less. Benchmarks on real tasks are the only fair comparison.
questions.intuitionTrap: A single big number feels like it must summarise performance.
questions.principle: Performance ≈ clock rate × work per cycle, across however many cores the task can use.
questions.funFact: In the 2000s, high-clocked Pentium 4 chips were often beaten by AMD Athlon 64 chips running at noticeably lower clock speeds.

questions.scenario: You load a website hosted on another continent.
questions.question: How does most of that data cross between continents?
questions.reveal: Through fibre-optic cables on the ocean floor.
questions.explanation: The vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic, often estimated at about 99%, travels through fibre-optic cables laid across the seabed, hundreds of them spanning well over a million kilometres in total. Each carries data as pulses of light at enormous rates. Satellites mostly serve places cables don't reach, and traditional satellites 36,000 km up add noticeable delay.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Wireless' everyday life makes us imagine the internet floating through the sky.
questions.principle: Optical fibre carries far more data, with lower delay, than radio links over long distances.
questions.funFact: Sharks have occasionally been filmed biting undersea cables, though fishing gear and ship anchors cause most damage.

questions.scenario: On a café's public Wi-Fi, you log in to a website showing the padlock icon (HTTPS).
questions.question: What can the café's network typically see?
options: Which site, but not what you send
questions.reveal: Usually which site you visit, but not what you send.
questions.explanation: HTTPS encrypts the content travelling between you and the site, including passwords, messages and the specific pages you view, so the café can't read it. But some metadata usually leaks: the domain name often appears in DNS lookups and in the first message of the encrypted connection, and the network can see how much data flows and when. So they may know you visited a site, not what you did there.
questions.intuitionTrap: Encryption feels all-or-nothing: either everything is hidden or nothing is.
questions.principle: TLS encrypts content, but metadata such as destination and traffic volume can still be visible.
questions.caveat: Newer techniques such as encrypted DNS and Encrypted Client Hello can hide the site name too, where both sides support them.
questions.funFact: The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the website itself is trustworthy: scam sites can have padlocks too.

questions.scenario: Your phone screen is showing a bright, pure-yellow image.
questions.question: Which colours of tiny lights in the screen are actually glowing?
questions.explanation: Almost every screen has only three kinds of sub-pixel: red, green and blue. There's no yellow light at all. Your eye has three types of colour-sensing cone, and red plus green light stimulates them in nearly the same way that true yellow light does, so your brain sees yellow. Look through a magnifying glass at a yellow patch and you'll see glowing red and green dots.
questions.intuitionTrap: We assume a screen shows a colour by emitting that colour.
questions.principle: Additive colour mixing: three primaries can mimic most colours because human colour vision has three channels.
questions.caveat: A few TVs have added yellow sub-pixels, but nearly all screens use just red, green and blue.
questions.funFact: To many animals with different colour vision, our screens' 'yellow' wouldn't look like yellow at all.

questions.scenario: An AI model correctly classifies 99% of patients when screening for a rare disease that affects 1% of people.
questions.question: Does that prove the model is good at spotting the disease?
options: No, it could miss every case
No, 99% is too low to use
questions.reveal: No: it could miss every single case.
questions.explanation: If only 1% of people have the disease, a 'model' that simply says 'healthy' to everyone is 99% accurate while catching zero cases. Accuracy hides this when one outcome is rare. To judge a screening model you need to know how many real cases it catches (sensitivity, or recall) and how many of its alarms are real (precision).
questions.intuitionTrap: A high percentage sounds like a strong result, whatever it's measuring.
questions.principle: With imbalanced classes, accuracy is misleading; use recall and precision.
questions.funFact: Fraud detection faces the same issue: genuine fraud is often well under 1% of transactions.

questions.scenario: Data in a fibre-optic cable travels as pulses of light.
questions.question: How fast does that light travel along the fibre?
options: Exactly the speed of light, c
questions.reveal: About two-thirds of the speed of light in a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Light slows down in glass. Fibre has a refractive index of about 1.47, so pulses travel at roughly 204,000 km per second rather than 300,000. Over long routes that adds measurable delay: about 5 milliseconds for every 1,000 km of fibre. Radio waves through air travel at very nearly the full speed of light, and can take straighter paths.
questions.intuitionTrap: 'Light' sounds like it always travels at 'the speed of light'.
questions.principle: Light's speed in a material is c divided by the material's refractive index.
questions.funFact: High-frequency traders built chains of microwave towers between Chicago and New York partly because radio through air beats light in glass.

questions.scenario: Password A is 8 characters chosen at random from all 94 keyboard symbols. Password B is 4 words chosen at random from a list of 7,776 common words.
questions.question: Against an attacker who knows exactly how each was generated, which is stronger?
questions.explanation: Strength comes from how many possibilities an attacker must try. A has 94⁸ ≈ 6 × 10¹⁵ options, about 52 bits. B has 7,776⁴ ≈ 3.7 × 10¹⁵, also about 52 bits, despite being made of ordinary words. Each random word adds about 12.9 bits, while each random symbol adds about 6.6. Add a fifth word and B pulls well ahead, while staying far easier to remember.
questions.intuitionTrap: Symbols and gibberish look strong; plain words look weak.
questions.principle: Password strength is the size of the space it was randomly drawn from, measured in bits of entropy.
questions.caveat: This only holds if the words are chosen randomly; a memorable phrase you picked yourself is far weaker.
questions.funFact: The 7,776-word list matches five rolls of a die (6⁵ = 7,776), the basis of the 'Diceware' method.

goDeeper.text: 8 × log₂94 ≈ 52.4 bits; 4 × log₂7,776 ≈ 51.7 bits; 5 words ≈ 64.6 bits.

questions.scenario: Your phone ignores your taps when you wear ordinary wool gloves.
questions.question: Why?
options: The screen senses your finger's charge
questions.reveal: The screen senses your finger's electrical properties, which the glove blocks.
questions.explanation: Most phone screens are capacitive: a grid of transparent electrodes holds a pattern of electric fields just above the glass. Your finger is a conductor full of salty water, so touching the screen disturbs the field and changes the capacitance at that spot. Wool is an insulator and keeps your finger too far away. Touchscreen gloves weave in conductive threads at the fingertips.
questions.intuitionTrap: Screens are 'touch' screens, so they seem to detect pressure.
questions.principle: Capacitive sensing detects a conductor changing an electric field, not pressure.
questions.funFact: A sausage can work your touchscreen, which some people in South Korea reportedly used in a cold winter.

questions.scenario: In JavaScript, Python and most other languages, you type: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
questions.question: Does it evaluate to true?
questions.explanation: Computers store these numbers in binary floating point. Just as 1/3 can't be written exactly in decimal, 0.1 and 0.2 can't be written exactly in binary, so each is stored as the nearest possible value. Their sum comes out as 0.30000000000000004, which isn't the same stored value as 0.3. Programmers compare floats with a small tolerance, or use decimal types for money.
questions.intuitionTrap: Computers are 'perfect at maths', so simple sums should be exact.
questions.principle: Binary floating point represents most decimal fractions only approximately.
questions.funFact: Rounding errors like this are why banking software usually counts money in whole cents rather than fractional dollars.

questions.scenario: A solar panel receives exactly the same strength of sunlight on a hot summer day and on a cold, clear winter day.
questions.question: On which day does it produce more electricity?
questions.explanation: Silicon solar cells become less efficient as they heat up: their voltage drops, costing very roughly 0.3–0.5% of output for every extra degree. A panel baking at 65 °C can lose well over 10% compared with the same panel at 25 °C. Sunlight brings energy, but heat is the enemy. Summer still usually wins overall because days are longer and the Sun is higher.
questions.intuitionTrap: Hot, sunny weather sounds like ideal solar conditions.
questions.principle: Semiconductor solar cells lose voltage, and so efficiency, as their temperature rises.
questions.funFact: Floating solar farms on reservoirs run a little cooler, and so slightly more efficiently, thanks to the water beneath them.

questions.scenario: You compress a large text document into a .zip file and it shrinks a lot. Then you zip the zip file.
questions.question: How much smaller does it get the second time?
questions.reveal: Barely changes, and may even get slightly bigger.
questions.explanation: Compression works by finding patterns and redundancy and describing them more briefly. The first pass removes most of that redundancy, so its output looks almost random. There's nothing left for a second pass to squeeze, and the extra headers can make the file slightly larger. In fact, no lossless method can shrink every possible file: there are more long files than short ones to map them to.
questions.intuitionTrap: If squeezing worked once, it seems like it should keep working.
questions.principle: Lossless compression removes redundancy; data without redundancy can't be compressed further.
questions.funFact: That's also why zipping photos or videos barely helps: JPEG and video formats are already compressed.

questions.scenario: On a freezing day outdoors, your phone shows 30% battery, then suddenly shuts down. Back inside and warm, it turns on again showing over 20%.
questions.question: What happened?
questions.reveal: Cold slowed the battery's chemistry, so it couldn't deliver power.
questions.explanation: A lithium-ion battery makes electricity through chemical reactions as lithium ions shuttle through a liquid electrolyte. Cold slows both, which raises the battery's internal resistance. When the phone asks for a burst of power, the voltage sags below what the phone needs and it shuts down to protect itself, even though charge remains. Warm the battery up and most of that 'lost' charge becomes usable again.
questions.intuitionTrap: A dead phone looks like an empty battery.
questions.principle: Lower temperature slows electrochemical reactions and ion transport, increasing internal resistance.
questions.caveat: Charging a lithium-ion battery below freezing can damage it, so many devices refuse to charge when very cold.
questions.funFact: Electric cars often warm their batteries before fast-charging in winter for the same reason.
